Last night I gave a presentation at [Carbon
5](http://www.carbonfive.com/ "Carbon 5") hack night
[meetup](http://www.meetup.com/Hack-Night-at-Carbon-Five-LA/). The
intention was to give an intro to natural language processing (NLP) and
Naive Bayes.  There’s a lot of different types NLP, but I thought that
the best way to introduce it in one night was to focus on Naive Bayes
classification and sequential probability estimation.  The examples I
used were classifying tweets into positive/negative/neutral/unsure
categories, and sequentially estimating the probability of emotions in
[EMO20Q](http://sail.usc.edu/emo20q "Emotion Twenty Questions"), which
I’ve been working on at hack night.

It was fun presenting about programming because in academic talks it
usually stops at the equations, while last night I got to go into the
details of how it is implemented in
[NLTK](http://code.google.com/p/nltk/), which I find very clever.  It
went well but I still had some constructive feedback.  By the end of the
talk I realized that I was using too many variations on the names of the
terms of Naive Bayes, like p(model\|data),  p(label\|feature), or
p(category\|word).  On one hand, I thought it would be good to inoculate
the audience to the different jargon, but I realized that it would have
been better to stick to one convention and save that jargon inoculation
to the end.

Thanks again to Carbon Five for hosting. I wish all presentations could
be accompanied by beer and pizza!
